In supervised learning, a simple approach can be effective by combining several basic components. However, in the context of offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), such a strategy isn't always successful, as it lacks consideration for valuable aspects within the offline dataset. A more comprehensive framework is necessary to ensure more reliable and consistent performance. This paper introduces a novel method called GAP (Learning From Good Paths in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning) that integrates three key elements from offline data: accurate state representations, well-executed action transitions, and neighboring states with high reward predictions. Experimental results on a range of multi-agent environments demonstrate that GAP consistently outperforms existing baselines in terms of stability and ease of use.

Radiation therapy treatment planning for cancer patients benefits from integrating soft-tissue contrast from MRI or CT images with high-resolution MV images obtained through radiotherapy. Although current MV images provide exceptional tissue contrast, their low spatial resolution and distorted quality hinder effective integration with other imaging modalities. A study revealed a method to enhance the alignment of 2D and 3D radiotherapy images by leveraging the contrast in MV images using a CNN-based approach. The study found that a 50% improvement in target detection accuracy could be achieved by training the CNN to identify soft-tissue landmarks in 2D radiotherapy images. Furthermore, the CNN demonstrated the ability to locate these landmarks with sub-pixel accuracy, even when presented with low-contrast and noisy radiography images. The study also found that a method to combine probabilistic landmark information outperformed traditional detection metrics, resulting in a 20% improvement in target localisation accuracy compared to the best existing approach.

For over a decade, a fundamental debate has surrounded the single-particle entanglement concept and its relevance to nonlocal phenomena. Some contend that the single-particle entanglement of a particle, say, in a superposition of localized states at positions a and b, is essentially equivalent to the state of an individual qubit and yields only the same nonlocal effect, namely the SteineraBell advantage. Conversely, some contend that it results in a more significant phenomenon, namely, single-particle steering capable of producing a genuinely nonlocal effect, namely, noncontextual advantage. In this work, we establish that the single-particle entanglement of a particle can indeed give rise to single-particle steering and a noncontextual advantage, as demonstrated via the tripartite contextuality scenario. Moreover, the magnitude of the achievable noncontextual advantage can be precisely quantified and exhibits a direct relationship with the degree of the single-particle (local) entanglement. Furthermore, the necessary and sufficient condition for a single-particle entangled particle to achieve the maximal noncontextual advantage in this scenario is also elucidated.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence technologies within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has the potential to revolutionize various applications, including intelligent transportation systems, autonomous driving, and traffic management systems. However, the open and shared nature of IoVs also exposes it to significant security and privacy risks stemming from malicious attacks and data breaches by untrustworthy nodes. To mitigate these concerns, research initiatives have turned to innovative decentralized learning frameworks that combine Federated Learning and Blockchain technologies. This specialized sub-literal review delves into the proposed Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning architectures for IoVs, examining the operational mechanisms, security and privacy safeguards, and critical challenges and open questions in this domain. By leveraging Blockchain technology, several research projects have successfully developed secure Blockchain-enabled FL frameworks for IoVs that encompass decentralized model training, data sharing, model aggregation, and decentralized model deployment systems. As the field continues to evolve, numerous open questions and future research directions are identified to guide the development of Blockchain-enabled FL applications for IoVs.

V392 Persei, a nova that recently peaked in brightness, is under intense scrutiny by astronomers.
V392 Persei originated from a dwarf nova, and its eruption exhibited unusually high X-ray and \gamma-ray brightness.
Spectral analysis of V392 Persei across radio to \gamma-ray frequencies allowed researchers to pinpoint the primary source of the nova's energy to neutrons bouncing off nuclei in the surrounding environment.
This level of energy output is exceptionally rare for novae and places recent observations of X-telescopes and dwarf novae in a new, extreme context.
Comparing V392 Persei to recent supernovae caused by white dwarfs, which typically have accreted from binary stars, reveals striking similarities.
However, V392 Persei stands out due to its forerunner emissions seen in X-rays and \gamma-rays, as well as its rapid rate of brightness decline.

A proposed enhancement to existing feedback methods for wireless communication systems involves using a set of signal precoders derived from Gaussian mixture models to reduce computation costs in real-time applications. In the proposed approach, base stations create these precoders in line with observed data conditions and embed a compact representation of the model into user devices, eliminating the need for field deployment of complex, real-time modeling algorithms. A concrete implementation using a robust statistical method, based on covariance matrix estimation, demonstrates how the model can be effectively utilized for encoding feedback and shows potential performance gains over current techniques. The proposed solution also paves the way for advanced applications in time-varying environments and removes the necessity for extensive channel probing in future system designs.

We perform detailed, comprehensive, three-dimensional simulations of a periodic system that includes a lattice, demonstrating the existence of stable, non-uniform, nonequilibrium surface currents in multiple dimensions under nonequilibrium conditions. These currents coexist with localized, equilibrium bulk states and remain isolated in momentum space. Our findings are validated through in-depth, comprehensive, comprehensive, graphical analyses in multiple dimensions and supported by simplified, analytically treatable, two-dimensional, isolated models. Furthermore, we outline potential, exotic, three-dimensional, nonequilibrium surface current applications.

Dynamic simulations of dark matter accretion onto black holes have been known for some time. Analytically, Bondi first derived a formula for steady-state accretion nearly seven decades ago. However, any potential deviation from the Bondi rate has significant implications for multiple fields of study, including early universe structure formation, the growth of supermassive black holes during the dawn of time, and constraints on small primordial black hole abundance. In this work, we develop two methods to estimate the rate of mass loss from a gas cloud due to gravity, likely generated by a black hole at its center. The first approach uses perturbative gravity to directly estimate the rate of mass loss from a spherical gas distribution, while the second employs time-dependent accretion simulations to estimate the rate of mass loss from a gas distribution subject to turbulent fluctuations. Both methods yield an estimate of the ratio between the actual accretion rate and the Bondi rate as a function of these fluctuations. As the intensity of the fluctuations increases, we observe that this ratio initially rises, peaks, and then declines, potentially enabling rapid black hole growth even when the local environment is losing a substantial amount of mass.

The earliest galaxies likely contained dense star clusters at their centers, and one type of these clusters, known as nuclear star clusters, may have resided within our own Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. Within these clusters, a dense collection of stars at their core, called remnant cores, could have formed from black holes that had lost their momentum. The interactions between these black holes in the star clusters could have generated detectable gravitational waves by LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA. Based on a detailed simulation, we predict a specific pattern of gravitational waves with a distinct feature, allowing us to differentiate between events occurring in dense star clusters and those in the rest of the universe. This signature could help scientists map the development of the early universe and potentially even identify a specific nuclear star cluster during gravitational wave observations.

In modern high-speed wireless networks, ensuring secure data transmission is a pressing concern. Physical layer security leverages the characteristics of wireless channels to mitigate this risk. To take full advantage of physical layer security techniques, high-speed wireless systems must be evaluated from the same perspective. Orthogonal access methods like OFDM, commonly used in these systems, have been shown to suffer from reduced security due to their multiplexing nature. As a result, non-orthogonal approaches have been proposed to improve the privacy of end users. However, these proposed methods have limited effectiveness in certain scenarios. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of physical layer security techniques in a more practical multi-carrier wireless scenario with an external attacker and a relay node. Two privacy-enhancing schemes based on time-switching and time-power splitting architectures are proposed and their performance is thoroughly analyzed and compared to the existing methods in terms of achievable secrecy capacity. Numerical results are presented to provide a clear understanding of the limitations of physical layer security in evaluating the security of OFDM systems.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving puzzles and planning.  One significant drawback of text-based games is their slow rendering speed of graphical elements, which results in a low scene update rate.  Our research reveals that the number of pixels required to depict certain types of puzzle games is quite minimal, often amounting to a few thousand pixels.  By taking full advantage of modern graphics processing capabilities, we developed TextWorldExpress, a revised version of the original text-based game library that allows for one-third of the puzzle games to be rendered at over 800,000 actions per second.  This breakthrough provides cutting-edge speeds of approximately 200 real-world seconds per million actions for specific complex puzzle games.  By incorporating high-thrux rendering speeds of TextWorldExpress into the original evaluation protocols, we introduced two new benchmarks that encompass a variety of challenging puzzle benchmarks.  When applied to popular artificial intelligence models of language and program generation, our new benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements of three to four orders of magnitude in training three models with limited data.

Deep learning methods, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved significant success in various sequential data processing tasks. However, their large size and complexity hinder their practical deployment on embedded devices for real-time applications. This research introduces a novel approach to optimizing LSTM networks for sequential video recognition by incorporating an algorithm and hardware design. The proposed optimized LSTM structure, along with a corresponding custom processing unit, aims to enhance the energy efficiency of video recognition while maintaining high accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with the resulting system outperforming existing optimized LSTM hardware implementations in terms of accuracy and energy consumption for sequential video recognition.

One key concept in holography is the gravity conjecture, which suggests that even a small amount of charge leads to an unstable state. Researchers have identified the origin of this instability by demonstrating that a particular type of charged operator is always non-convex under specific conditions. This non-convexity is in direct opposition to the linearized gravity's ability to curve spacetime in a manner consistent with the positive energy condition. Furthermore, the operator's two-point correlation function exhibits behavior indicative of a highly unstable state when the amount of charge surpasses a threshold, thus providing support for the gravity conjecture.

In positive characteristic, we investigate the behavior of the Hilbert polynomial of the test ideal $\mathcal{J}(I^n)$ in relation to the ideal $I$ and the power $p$. Specifically, we define a new characteristic of F-finiteness for local rings based on the stability of the test ideal's associated graded ring. We prove that this characteristic is also applicable to the divisorial ideal $\mathcal{I}(I^n)$ and F-jump ideal $\gamma(I^n)$. Additionally, we establish that a certain condition on the test ideal is equivalent to the ring being strongly F-regular. Notably, this condition is also equivalent to the associated graded ring being F-regular for any ideal. This characteristic is invariant under the property of being F-regular for the associated graded ring with respect to the divisorial ideal and jump ideal. Furthermore, we establish that a certain condition on the test ideal is equivalent to the ring having a property of F-purity with respect to the associated graded ring with respect to the divisorial ideal and jump ideal. This condition is also applicable to the ring's property of being F-rational with respect to the associated graded ring with respect to the test ideal and divisorial ideal and jump ideal.

The integration of auxiliary services into energy markets is an important aspect of policy design for energy system reliability. To effectively shape the rules and RFPs for auxiliary services procurement, research on RAR interactions is essential. However, an abstract level model used in previous research fails to account for the actual quantity offered in addition to the price, an element that plays a key role in the auxiliary services market. To address this limitation, the current study presents a new model of RFP interactions at a more concrete level, providing valuable insights for the design of energy system support policies. The model reveals that R interactions are complex and can take various forms, including both negative and positive effects. It also highlights the need to consider the actual quantity offered in order to accurately assess market interactions. The implications of the model are tested through numerical examples, which demonstrate its practical relevance for energy policy design.

Let F and G be two polynomials within the set C_q[x], where C_q denotes a finite field. The composition of these polynomials is defined as F(G(x)). A polynomial F is considered post-critical if the iterated composition G^n(F(x)) results in a polynomial with integer coefficients from the field for all non-negative integers n. A notable characteristic of post-critical polynomials is that, when the field has a prime order, the set of its coefficients also consists of prime numbers. A notable exception to this rule is the polynomial -x^2 in fields with two elements. A polynomial G is said to be compatible with the set of prime numbers when the composition G^n(x) produces an polynomial with integer coefficients from the field for all non-negative integers n. A significant finding reveals that if the degree of F is at least two, the result is guaranteed to be post-critical, whereas if the degree of F is one, a condition is established under which the result is guaranteed to be compatible with the set of prime numbers. A notable example of a polynomial that results in infinite iterated compositions when the degree of F is one is given as x - 1/2 in a field with three elements. As the seasons change on the outer planets, their polar atmospheres experience significant transformations. During the summer, a temporary low-pressure system forms at the pole as the sun reaches its highest point in the sky. On Saturn, these vortexes are easily seen due to their large size and can be studied in great detail. However, a significant number of Saturn's polar stratospheric polar vortexes have been found to occur within a hexagonal cloud pattern during the approaching warm season at its north pole. Researchers have found that these hexagons, which form as a result of strong atmospheric currents, are strongly associated with the upcoming warm season rather than the upcoming polar vortex. By using various data sources, the current study aims to understand the ongoing polar atmospheric conditions on Saturn's north pole and found that the polar vortex is in the process of forming as of now. The research also found that the position of the polar vortex is likely to shift outside of the northern hexagon in the coming weeks.

Consider a Schrödinger equation within an exterior domain, an area outside a bounded, smooth convex region in n-dimensional space where n is at least two dimensions. The equation is given an initial condition within this area and a zero condition at infinity. The question of whether the solution's mass can grow infinitely large in a finite time period is an active area of research. This paper provides an active area of research by proving the existence periods during which the solution's mass is infinite and beyond that point no solution exists.

The concept of local uniform reduction is employed to characterize varieties defined over a $Q$-algebra in terms of various families of one-parameter subvarieties over the same base. In this context, it has been established that if the set of subvarieties over which a carefully produced variety yields a non-ruled fiber over the base is finite, then this variety is equivalent to a direct sum of Ruled varieties over the same base family. Conversely, if this local sum is not present at a particular point, then this point is associated with a specific subvariety of the same family. These statements hold true for varieties produced over a $Q$-algebra in characteristic zero, and a significant extension of these results has been achieved to include those produced over the same base in characteristic $p > 0$.

We suggest a new covariant framework that extends the familiar bundle grading framework, adapting it to a smooth setting. This new structure, called a graded bundle, generalizes the concept of a Lie algebroid and provides a framework that includes both symplectic and Poisson bundle concepts. We demonstrate how various relations and projections within these graded bundles can be defined and studied within this cohesive framework.

Let G be a reductive group defined over a field K. This paper explores local factors in the theory of G-schemes over rings, specifically examining the properties of integrals denoted as $\Omega(f^\Omega)$. We analyze these integrals in the context of G, particularly when K is a local field or a p-adic field. Additionally, we address the challenges in extending the theory of automorphic forms from G(K) to GL_n over the field of rational numbers. These challenges involve understanding the behavior of these integrals in relation to GL_n and understanding how to adjust the measures used in the theory.

The advanced capabilities of synchrotron radiation sources, particularly in x-ray scattering, have transformed the study of non-equilibrium dynamics in complex liquids. A particularly challenging aspect of this field is measuring molecular structure and spatial changes during the nuclear network formation process. By leveraging x-ray resonance scattering, a more effective approach has been developed to analyze these dynamics. This technique enables the precise tracking of transient structural phases that occur after photo-induced bond breaking. As a result, recent experiments have revealed a brief period of structural over-saturation, lasting approximately 200 picoseconds, which is followed by a 2-nanosecond relaxation phase. These findings are expected to significantly enhance our comprehension of complex liquids from a molecular perspective.

We present a new mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured porous media, where the geometry of the system is discretized using a non-matching grid. In this approach, we find the pressure across a simplified, star-shaped geometry using a mixed HM-SR method and a localized, triangular fractured region using a discrete Galerkin approach. Our model preserves mass conservation locally and globally, and also keeps computational expenses low by reducing the number of unknown variables. Our numerical experiments highlight the model's high accuracy, efficient computation, and mass conservation properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our numerical model can accurately simulate the flow in a fractured reservoir and maintain a high level of mass conservation.

Hypothesis testing in science frequently relies on Bayes factors, yet their
interpretation can be ambiguous. Stein's paradox highlights the challenge of specifying
precise hypotheses in large-scale scientific studies with numerous data points or
potential hypotheses. This document explores various approaches to address this
issue, primarily centered on defining broader hypothesis spaces and developing
methods to prioritize within these spaces, including using Bayes factors itself.
Moreover, we advocate for the adoption of Bayes factors in priority specification
and develop a structured framework for integrating Bayes factors in scientific
investigations, emphasizing the value of repeated studies with differing prior
conditions. Ultimately, we illustrate the utility of this framework through the
analysis of prior research and discoveries in particle physics and cosmology.

This time period has seen significant investment in developing artificial intelligence systems capable of mimicking human-like interactions, particularly discourse functional artificial intelligence. These devices heavily rely on discrete indicators such as "in fact," "however," and "consequently" to convey their grasp of a subject to a broader audience. Despite their utility in guiding human understanding of complex topics, these indicators must convey genuine semantic coherence, as opposed to mere statistical correlations. Current examination methods for the semantic meaning behind these indicators are limited, necessitating a more robust approach. To address this limitation, we present Discourse Semantic Tree, a systematic framework for evaluating the meaning behind these indicators. To showcase the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to several existing models and compare the results with a baseline method. Our findings reveal that this examination method yields results that demonstrate greater semantic relevance compared to existing methods.

When performing matrix factorization to solve complex tasks like matrix completion and collaborative filtering, a common approach is to constrain the solution space by assuming a low dimension. Although previous studies have highlighted the existence of a favorable optimization landscape under this constraint, the underlying geometric properties that contribute to this convexity-like behavior have not been fully explored. In the present work, we address this knowledge gap by analyzing the geometry of the solution space for low-dimension matrix factorization in detail. A geodesic distance metric is used to characterize the geometry, and we find that the solution space is geodesically convex, with a strictly positive curvature. The geodesic distance between any two points in the space is directly proportional to the Frobenius distance between the corresponding matrices, with a constant of proportionality of 1/2. Furthermore, the minimum geodesic distance from any point in the space to the set of matrices that yield the same output as the point is bounded below by the rank of the point divided by 2. These findings have significant implications for understanding and developing non-convex matrix optimization methods, as a gradient descent algorithm with an appropriately chosen step size exhibits global convergence to a minimum.

In 1983, Goldberg and Seymour proposed a conjecture stating that for any bipartite graph G with no subgraph having three disjoint cycles, the edge chromatic number is at most the sum of the maximum and minimum degree divided by two. We identify a bipartite graph with such a property and demonstrate that its edge chromatic number exceeds this sum to two times its average degree divided by two, providing a counterexample to the original conjecture. Additionally, we show how modifying the lower bound to two times the average degree results in a set of graphs, one of which can be made into a valid configuration that edge-coloring four-times 3-edge-colorable. This indicates that resolving the current issue may require a more precise lower bound involving the sum of the maximum and second maximum degree divided by two for graphs with no subgraph having three disjoint cycles.

This study employs coevolutionary genetic algorithms to reach a Nash Equilibrium in a simple symmetric Cournot game where multiple firms compete by determining production levels of a homogeneous good. To do this, a non-learning policy is developed for each of the multiple firms participating in the competition. Coevolutionary genetic algorithms are then used to determine the number of firms in the market and the size of the population of these firms. We find that these algorithms successfully create a stable, rational strategy for the entire population of the first firm and a smaller population of the second, but fail to do so for the third. To address this, co-op encoding is implemented to reduce the second population size to one and a third approach is tested for the third, but neither yields satisfactory results.

Let O(G) represent a weighted directed graph whose edges form a set of assumptions for a specific polynomial ideal, specifically B. If the edge pattern of O(G) results in the ideal being matched with the directed graph G's square-free edge ideal, then O(G) is considered typical in relation to B. This concept is then extended to the symbolic power scenario, if n-th symbolic and ordinary powers of B align for O(G) and G respectively, especially for n >= 2. This study investigates the class of directed graph ideals by examining two properties of O(G): being typical and being symbolic typical. It is proven that both being typical and being symbolic typical ensure the ideal's reduction in B's depth when analyzed sequentially, and it is demonstrated that these properties are preserved when raised to any positive integer power. Additionally, this study provides a limited class of directed graph ideals that are both typical and symbolic typical, and it is shown that being typical and being symbolic typical are distinct characteristics.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely adopted in vision tasks due to their high accuracy, but concerns have been raised about the safety of their deployments in critical applications such as self-driving cars. Researchers have previously tested CNN reliability by subjecting them to adversarial attacks and hardware faults, but these methods have limitations. Adversarial inputs do not mirror real-world hardware failures, and fault-injection results may be skewed by introduced injection errors and unaccounted noise variations. To overcome these issues, this work introduces a novel framework for establishing a hardware-resilient CNN reliability case, building on the case-based approach. Within this framework, previous adversarial and fault-injection tests are categorized as support elements, and it defines additional test types to gather more comprehensive evidence. Moreover, this paper investigates the theoretical basis for using activation thresholds to limit the impact of hardware faults on CNN outputs, demonstrating their value in securing CNNs against hardware failures.

The Jordanian twist, first introduced in 1996, is a deformation of the co-Frobenius structure that has been extensively researched in recent years due to its relevance in the context of quantum group representations. However, existing studies have treated the parameter as a generic constant, neglecting its inherent inherent nature. In this study, we investigate the impact of a varying parameter on the Jordanian twist, leading to the identification of a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists with distinct properties. Our analysis reveals that the Jordan twist, modified by this parameter family, results in altered reciprocity laws and obstructs the applicability of the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction for obtaining a semi-simple category from the representation category. These findings have been supported by numerical evidence obtained through direct computation.

Clustering is a widely used technique for organizing large datasets into meaningful groups. Languages that rely on context-free morphology can create a shared vocabulary space by combining the semantic information from clustered words. The crucial point is that the resulting vocabulary must be consistent across speakers of different languages. In this paper, we address the challenge of constructing a common semantic area from multiple languages without clear cluster boundaries. The proposed method involves a three-step process: first, we obtain language-specific word embeddings and then train separate area components by treating them as isolated monolingual datasets; finally, we ensure that the combined semantic area works effectively for each individual language. The evaluation results show the proposed approach outperforms existing techniques in tasks that involve switching between different languages during testing.

This research examines the production of various particle types, including pions, kaons, protons, anti-protons, and phi mesons, produced in high-energy Xe-Xe collisions at the CSDS. Observations were made across different transverse momentum ranges and collision centralities. Similar production patterns were found for particles of comparable mass, both in terms of their mass distributions and those of transverse momentum. In more central collisions, a slight shift towards higher transverse momenta was noted for heavier particles when compared to lighter ones, a finding consistent with previous studies in p-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions. Additionally, the ratio of proton to pion production remained largely unchanged for both Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions of the same energy and centralities, despite slight variations in particle yields for different masses. The measured production ratios of protons to pions and anti-protons to pions, along with the average transverse momentum values, were also compared to predictions made using the PYTHIA 8.22 simulation, taking into account both soft and pT-dependent hard scattering processes.

In November 2019, Chile experienced widespread unrest fueled by anti-government demonstrations, which escalated following the murder of 18-year-old student Catalina Saavedra in Santiago. Despite ongoing protests, the Chilean president resigned in mid-December, giving way to temporary governance. To comprehend the complexities of these events, a mathematical model was developed, drawing on reported statistics and providing a detailed examination of the protests' dynamics in Santiago over time. Notably, an analogy was made between the spread of unrest and an epidemic, with 'unrest' serving as a contagious agent. A key characteristic of the 2019 unrest in Santiago was its spatial variability, rendering conventional epidemic models inadequate due to their reliance on homogeneous population assumptions. Consequently, a novel model was created to capture the spatial spread of unrest within Santiago's three main neighborhoods: the east, central, and west. The model's parameters were calibrated using available data, revealing the east as the origin of unrest, with the central area acting as the primary conduit for its transmission to the west. Ultimately, an interpretative discussion was offered to contextualize the model's model outcomes.

This research focuses on creating a method to identify subregular expressions that encompass given alternating regular expressions, which are commonly used specifications in various fields, including web security, firewall configuration, and protocol analysis. By categorizing five prevalent alternatives to alternating expressions as extensions with iterated single characters, we developed a solver utilizing Presburger Arithmetic and employed Clarke's closure operator to achieve this purpose. Following this approach, we created an alternative expression tool and surveyed its effectiveness compared to existing solutions, showing that it can successfully handle real-world cases.

This study aims to address the challenge of mobile agent localization using fusion of inertial and depth sensors. The complexity of real-world sensor data often poses significant challenges for traditional processing methods, particularly in terms of accuracy and efficiency. To tackle these difficulties, we introduce a novel external memory attention neural network algorithm, designed to efficiently process high-dimensional inertial and optical sensor data. The proposed method incorporates an initial network to extract compact sensor features, followed by the integration of an external memory attention neural network for precise pose estimation. The proposed method was evaluated on multiple public datasets including KITTI, IMU, and SUNRGB-D, and the results indicate substantial improvements in localization accuracy compared to existing high-performance methods. The source code for the proposed method is available for download at https://github.com/leehongzhang/DeepVisualInertialLocalizationExternalMemoryAttention.

The concept of effective Hamiltonians is employed to establish a revised framework for identifying and understanding novel quantum material phases. By expanding upon the standard definition of symmetry-protected topological phases, we introduce new distinct phases of matter, specifically "higher-order topological Weyl point" and "higher-order topological charged gapless point" that can give rise to new material states of matter known as "higher-order Weyl materials". These new phases of matter exhibit "higher-order Fermi arc" states on their boundaries and "helical quadrupole surface hinge" states on their edges. We provide the theoretical underpinnings for these phases of matter, including their classification, as well as a practical method for calculating them based on expanded topological invariants derived from topological hologivity from several material candidates.

This study investigates the numerical resolution of a completion problem for Maxwell's equations, specifically the inverse time-dependent problem where a partial source and boundary measurement are given. A method combining H^1_0 x L^2 regularization and a Riemann-Liouville fractional integral is proposed to address this ill-posed problem. Furthermore, a iterative quadratic convergence algorithm is derived based on the proposed method's initial approximation. In order to obtain more accurate solutions, the solution from this algorithm can be integrated into the iteratively truncated total least squares iteration scheme. The stability of these two iterations is theoretically established, and numerous numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods. The results from these simulations indicate that the iterative quadratic convergence method and the iteratively truncated scheme successfully solve the data completion problem for the Maxwell equations.

The rapidly expanding size of data and models poses a significant challenge for the deployment of machine learning in mobile and mobile mobile devices. In order to overcome this limitation, we propose a novel framework for knowledge sharing among devices called Federated Selective Collection (FedGain). This framework allows a central server to share a subset of its data with a carefully chosen group of servers, which then train a model that can be deployed on mobile devices. We analyze the sample efficiency of this framework and devise a FedGain protocol that ensures the accuracy of the model can be maintained despite the fact that the combined data set is smaller than a single server's data set. The proposed FedGain protocol is tested in a real-world scenario for image classification on mobile devices and shows that it can achieve high accuracy with a relatively small amount of data.

It has been demonstrated that there are always rank increase elliptic curve quartic extensions of the rationals within the $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Furthermore, it has been proven that for any elliptic curve over the rationals with a reduction of at least 2 at the prime 2, there is an $S_4$ quartic extension of the rationals in which the p-adic valuation of the Tate-Shafarevich set is at least 2. Additionally, it has been shown that there are limited $A_4$ and $S_4$ quartic extensions of the rationals in which the expected average elliptic curve rank is at least 2, and there is an algorithm to identify them all.

We establish a new constraint on the entanglement growth rate in a spatially symmetric region, analogous to the quantum null energy condition (QNEC), specifically tailored for null-symmetric regions in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFT2). Three distinct methods are employed to derive this constraint, each offering unique insights and potentially providing a novel approach to conformal field theory. Furthermore, this constraint is shown to be a fundamental component of quantum null thermodynamics, enabling us to analyze two well-known holographic models, the End-of-the-World (ETW) bridge and the Gao-Jafferis-Wall (GJW) wormhole. As a result, we can re-express the dynamics of matter within these models in terms of local quantities, specifically the null stress and entropy flux, and demonstrate how they give rise to surges in the geometry, manifesting as 3-spheres within Anti-de Sitter (AdS) space and defectless wormholes, respectively. Ultimately, the influence of a double-null shock on the AdS/CFT correspondence is highlighted, where the bulk dynamics are governed by the transformation of a small CFT2 into an ensemble of nearly conformal theories, accompanied by the formation of BPS states and the entanglement of the original system with a thermal bath.

In order to ascertain the minimum time interval required for a given quantum state to transform into an indistinguishable version of itself through unitary evolution, known as the distinguishability duration (DD), researchers are examining various approaches. A recent study focuses on determining the relationship between two specific types of asymmetry, J-and Weyl-Cahill-Hillery (JC-H) asymmetries, and the DD within the confines of a single qubit's Bloch sphere. The study establishes a direct proportionality between the DD and the square of the shortest asymmetry, providing a more restricted yet equally valid inequality of the JC-H inequality. Moreover, research reveals that the DD is uncorrelated with other available asymmetries in the Bloch sphere, including the Fubini-Study (FS) and Weyl (W) asymmetries. In order to address this, the concept of a new asymmetry, the hyper-asymmetry, is introduced and demonstrated to have a direct correlation with the DD. In the context of the Bloch sphere, the relationship between the hyper-asymmetry, the FS asymmetry, and the W asymmetry is expressed through a set of inequalities. If $X$ is a given finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ and $Y$ is another space with additional smoothness, we are often interested in constructing an approximation space $W$ that combines the properties of both. Specifically, if $X$ has a small dimension and $Y$ has a large dimension, we can use an interpolation method to build $W$. This involves choosing an interpolation projector $P$ from $X$ and a Whitney extension operator $Q$ from $Y$, and defining $W$ as the set of functions that can be expressed as a linear combination of $P$ and $Q$. As a result, $W$ has a dimension equal to the sum of the dimensions of $X$ and $Y$, and we can establish certain approximation properties for $W$ based on the norms of $P$ and $Q$. In this study, we examine two interpolation projects commonly used in practice and derive bounds for their respective norms, which can be used to establish quantitative estimates for the smoothness of $W$.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material defects that cause decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to investigate the local dielectric properties and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, which are key components of superconducting quantum processors. A terahertz scanning probe creates an in-plane magnetic field that influences quantum Hall edge currents, revealing variations in carrier density and unexpected near-field signals around the microwave transmission lines. Furthermore, a simple method is demonstrated to correct etch-induced etalon effects in measuring dielectric constants, ensuring more accurate quantum processor materials. The study provides comprehensive terahertz nanoscopy data to facilitate the continued advancement of low-loss quantum processors.

This article provides an overview of the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere and surface conditions, with a focus on the interaction between the atmosphere and the surface. It critically examines the main theories and proposed mechanisms that could account for the extreme heat of the planet, with surface temperatures exceeding 500 degrees Celsius. It discusses various processes, such as atmospheric heat transport, solar wind interactions, and atmospheric composition changes, that may have contributed to the planet's current state. It also considers the role of slow tectonic processes, mantle convection, and volcanic activity in the long-term development of the atmosphere. The article highlights the complexity of these interactions and the need for a comprehensive understanding of the coupled atmosphere-lithosphere system. It calls for new space missions to Venus to conduct long-term observations and better understand the slow evolution of the planet, with a view towards planning for future missions like the Venera-D.

We developed a Bayesian approach to analyze the nonlinear time-dependent
Hawkes process, incorporating Gaussian process regression to model the complex
hinge function and hedge. A key challenge in this method is efficiently computing
the Bayesian estimates and inference due to its computational demands. 
To overcome this, a variational inference approach was used to obtain a computationally
efficient and flexible estimate. Our method's performance was evaluated through 
simulation studies and real-world applications, demonstrating its ability to accurately
capture the Hawkes process characteristics.

The interaction between high-intensity lasers and magnetized plasmas has the potential to simultaneously generate a new class of polarized gamma rays.  This process can also lead to significant amplification of the resulting gamma rays while overcoming the limitations of previous methods.  A new, efficient technique has been developed to achieve this simultaneous effect on a massive scale, capable of manipulating $10^{18}$ photons and magnetic fields of up to 50 Teslas.  This approach can be used to create a wide range of applications, including simultaneous control of the polarization and the intensity of deeply penetrating gamma rays, which can be applied to gamma microscopy and other forms of gamma-based imaging.

Quantum Electrodynamics predicts that a tau lepton has an extremely small electric dipole moment, valued at 4.88 times 10^-28 e cm according to two previous calculations. However, experimental efforts to set tighter limits on the tau lepton's electric dipole moment require accounting for new physics beyond the Standard Model. In order to do this, researchers must consider possible contributions from various sources, such as supersymmetry and left-symmetric models. By comparing the predicted contributions to the current experimental upper limit, scientists can constrain the parameter space of these models and explore connections to other exotic phenomena, such as CP violation in neutrino oscillations. Additionally, researchers have calculated the contribution to the tau lepton's electric dipole moment from neutrino see-saw mechanisms, finding that it is negligible in both the type-I and type-II see-saw variants.

We investigate decoding of rank-metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric decoding region. For a broad class of codes, including all linear codes, we examine the rank metric's symmetric decoding problem with a known symmetric error vector. A decoding algorithm is proposed that correctly recovers the message vector given a sufficiently small rank of the error vector, specifically less than min{d_ℓ^sr(C), ⌈K/2⌉}, where d_ℓ^sr denotes the leading singleton bound, and K represents the field size. Moreover, our method can reduce the rank of certain codes' vulnerable regions by up to one-fifth of what is achievable with existing techniques.

In this work, we examine the structure of conformal blocks within the operator product expansion in the context of two-dimensional CFTs on the sphere, focusing on cases where anti-holomorphic contributions are neglected. We investigate the conditions under which the conformal block can be identified with a piece of the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ theory's exchange diagram. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of this exchange diagram representation for the AdS$_3$ bulk action, particularly in relation to the Fierz–Jordan term. Additionally, we explore the properties of "double-twist" operators associated with this term. If we were to drop an assumption, the AdS$_3$ theory would then be accurately described by the Gravitational AdS/CFT correspondence.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a combinatorial method for calculating Pontrjagin classes, which were previously defined in a geometric way. However, when examining the combinatorial formula for the $2n$-th Pontrjagin class, a discrepancy surfaced between the combinatorial definition and the established one, as the values did not match even after considering variations in $p$ and applying factors of $\pi^ {2n}$. This research investigates the root cause of this mismatch, offering both a correction to the combinatorial expression and an in-depth exploration of the underlying reasons for the difference, which turn out to be attributable to specific contributions that arise $2$-dimensionally. Furthermore, related combinatorial coefficients are examined in a broader context.

The SN occurred in an N-type dwarf galaxy and a star-forming region of SN 2020jfo was relatively compact. The research team found the spectroscopic features typical of SN II, including a strong P Cygni profile in the H-alpha line, as well as unique characteristics of host galaxy N-type dwarfs, such as UV-optical infrared emission. The analysis of the spectra revealed unusual characteristics of SN 2020jfo's ejecta, with a wide range of hydrogen and helium velocities and an abundance of iron-peak elements and cobalt-56. The development of large-scale X-ray monitoring systems with wide viewing angles is hindered by the difficulty in creating screens that cover the ground effectively in multiple layers. This research proposes a new method for achieving this, known as a multiplexed lobster-eye structure, which combines many small devices and enables a system with a very large field of view. However, the existing versions of these structures have limited efficiency due to their solid packaging. Since nature's version of a lobster-eye structure is highly open, this project aims to mimic it using a new design that uses a dense arrangement of small mini-structure lobster-eye devices housed within a protective container. This design significantly improves light efficiency while maintaining a wide viewing range. The suitability of this design for its intended purpose is demonstrated using both computer simulations and mathematical analysis, and it significantly improves light efficiency significantly compared to the existing design.

We define a level set formulation of partial uniform ellipticity for non-linear operators and examine its relationship with the standard definition of partial uniform ellipticity. Additionally, this level set definition of ellipticity can be applied to non-differentiable functions, making it useful in various contexts, including the standard ellipticity of non-smooth non-linear operators, the bilevel level set type optimization of elliptic PDE eigenvalue problems, and the level set type optimization of advection-diffusion eigenvalue problems.

Our investigation into the theoretical framework of the cosmic speed field (ScField) employs deep learning techniques to substitute the complex ScField equations with a neural network, allowing us to explore the formation of dark matter halos within different cosmological models. Utilizing the SPHINX code, we simulated 120 N-body dark matter halo snapshots and found that a speed field generated by galaxy formation physics impacts the distribution of dark matter halos, particularly in the high mass tail, leading to a 0.1 to 0.2 magnitude shift compared to standard $\Lambda$CDM predictions. A neural network trained to identify halos in simulation data can also detect this effect and even predict it in new simulated data sets. Furthermore, we found that the effect of the ScField varies across different scales and can be more pronounced in modified dark energy models than in dark matter self-interaction models. This research highlights the potential of combining deep learning with theoretical physics to explore the formation of cosmic structures and suggests that the ScField may leave a detectable signature in observations of the distribution of dark matter halos.

We have developed a numerical method to simulate the evolution of rotating stars in the context of general relativity. This method uses a new mathematical formulation that enables more stable time-step calculations for slowly rotating stars by directly enforcing a key physical constraint - the conservation of angular momentum within each part of the star. This improvement builds upon an existing numerical method, and includes a new way to manage this angular momentum constraint using a modified physical variable and updated calculations. Our method demonstrates better accuracy and numerical stability compared to the original method, particularly when used with a common numerical technique to solve the resulting equations.

The surge of visually rich documents such as invoices, contracts, and receipts has created a significant opportunity and challenge for enterprise automation. The intricate nature of these documents has led to a new task known as visual document understanding, with a focus on practical applications like extracting useful information. The prevailing approach in this field, called trained-on-docs, involves creating employee-level annotations on the documents themselves. Although this method has produced promising results in specific use cases, its scalability is severely limited due to its high costs and time-consuming nature when dealing with various visually rich documents. The authors of the proposed model, called one-doc-less, aim to achieve significant cost savings and efficiency by leveraging easily accessible web data for the initial training, and then using extremely inexpensive tree-walk annotations to adapt the pre-trained model to specific visually rich documents. The authors' experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves comparable performance to the prevailing method with up to 99% less complex annotations and 95% less costs, while also achieving superior performance in multiple other scenarios. The proposed framework is designed to be broadly applicable to multiple visually rich documents and holds significant potential for the practical deployment of real-world document processing.

Astronomical observations in the multi-messenger spectrum, involving electromagnetic radiation, neutrinos, and gravitational waves, have a limited neutron star-neutron star and neutron star-black hole merger detection capability due to their sensitivity and distance constraints. Gravitational wave observatories, such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA, have a significant latency issue in identifying and classifying neutron star mergers associated with short gamma-ray bursts and electromagnetic afterglows. A machine learning approach, employing supervised classification techniques and transformer models, has been developed to address these limitations by efficiently detecting and categorizing electromagnetic burst events based on their light curves. A deep learning framework processes time-series data from three key parameters, including flux, color, and saturation, to reduce dimensionality and enhance classification performance. The proposed model achieved superior accuracy in identifying and classifying NS-NS and BNS mergers, outperforming existing methods in simulated gravitational wave detection scenarios. A significant reduction in computational cost and inference time, along with robust performance across different observatory data, has been demonstrated, providing a practical solution for real-time multi-messenger astronomy analysis.

Social interactions in cities are influenced by individuals' willingness to interact within urban environments. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this aspect was significantly affected. This study used mobile phone data from 12 urban areas in Brazil to analyze the diversity of urban encounters in terms of socioeconomic backgrounds. It was found that cities with more income diversity in social interactions showed a greater reduction in the size of these interactions during the pandemic compared to cities with less diversity. This effect was more pronounced in cities with a larger population and was observed in both metropolitan and non-metropolitan areas. Furthermore, this finding held true for areas with high and low population density. These social interactions were discovered to be correlated with the level of income diversity in the surrounding population, rather than just within the specific mobile phone population being studied. This effect was not observed in areas with high and low population density when the study was controlled for reductions in social mobility. This study highlights the critical role that the COVID-19 pandemic played in revealing the diversity of urban encounters and its impact on the socioeconomic benefits provided by living in cities.

The nature of early-universe star formation remains uncertain, with two competing theories suggesting that the first stars either predominantly formed at a high mass or accumulated mass in episodic bursts before collapsing to form low mass stars. Observations of massive protostars in the high-redshift universe have been used to investigate the mechanisms behind their growth rates. A simulation was conducted to examine the growth of a $10^3$ cubic parsec region around a high-z massive protostar over a 10 million year period, focusing on a 100 cubic parsec sphere centered on a high mass progenitor. The simulation revealed that external gas was too hot and thin to effectively supply the sphere through accretion shocks, but internal turbulence generated sufficient momentum transport to limit star formation within the sphere, resulting in the protostar growing in a closed system with little to no growth outside. The limited supply of external gas could be overcome in regions with high gas temperatures, and the confinement of the sphere could be overcome in regions with high turbulence, both of which were observed in high-z star-forming regions. The simulation also revealed that the sphere would undergo gravitational collapse within a few million years, leading to the formation of dense cores around the central protostar or through mergers of existing cores. This research extends our prior work, which established a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation framework for interacting water currents and oceanic surface waves, by setting the water current to a uniform velocity. Under this assumption, we analyze the Dysthe equation's ability to model wave-wave interactions in a body of water with constant current velocity, boundary conditions, and the conservation of water with varying depths. By applying a Crank-Nicolson scheme, we demonstrate that the Dysthe equation maintains key physical properties, including the conservation of water, wave interactions that stem from water depth, and the ability to handle both open and closed boundary conditions. Furthermore, we investigate how the distribution of water, the depth of the ocean, and the constant velocity of the current contribute to the persistence of waves.
